Task 2 — Santa Clara Residential Coverage Audit

Residential baseline (usecode 1,2,3,4,6) from ca_santa_clara_parcel_build_opt.gpkg compared to PostgreSQL public.unidata. City grouping uses normalized scity only (no city fallback), with hyphen normalization.

Executive summary

What leadership needs to know before scrolling the tables.

  • Residential coverage: 99.99% of county residential baseline parcels (453,215 of 453,276) appear in PostgreSQL public.unidata when both sides share the same normalized scity and parcel number (parcelnumb, trimmed and case-normalized).
  • Unmatched baseline: 61 residential baseline rows still lack that combined match—often scity label drift or missing ingest rows rather than literal absence of the parcel everywhere.
  • Where we measure attributes: The cards in Table 3 summarize one row count per normalized scity present in Unidata—34 buckets in this snapshot.
  • Soft spots in the schema: The weakest populated column overall right now is fhszsra (2.43%) (see Table 5 for more).

The KPI tiles directly above mirror these bullets; the How to read each table section next defines every column.

How to read each table

Short definitions so finance, product, and GIS readers interpret numbers the same way.

Snapshot tiles (under the blue header)

Residential coverageMatched baseline rows ÷ total residential baseline rows. Uses only **`scity` + `parcelnumb`** matches.
Baseline rowsResidential parcels in the county GeoPackage baseline (`usecode` 1,2,3,4,6) with a usable parcel number.
Matched in UnidataBaseline rows that found a partner row in Unidata with the same normalized `scity` and parcel number.
MissingBaseline rows that did not find such a partner.

Table 1 — Coverage by scity

Place (scity)Normalized situs city label for the row. Taken from **`scity` only** (blank → “(NULL)”); hyphens become spaces; spacing and case normalized.
Baseline rowsResidential parcels in the GeoPackage for this `scity` key.
Unidata rows (scity)All Unidata rows carrying this normalized `scity` (not limited to residential unless you filter separately).
MatchedBaseline residential rows whose parcel number appears in Unidata under the **same** normalized `scity`.
MissingBaseline residential rows in this bucket without such a match.
Coverage %Matched ÷ Baseline rows when baseline > 0. Gray styling means zero baseline residential rows (nothing to score).

Table 2 — Field completeness matrix

FieldColumn name on `unidata`.
TypeHow we evaluate presence (text vs numeric vs boolean vs array).
PresentRows that satisfy the “populated” rule for that field.
TotalAll rows in `unidata` for this export.
Completeness %Present ÷ Total. Colors highlight excellent → weak tiers.

sqft and building_area treat 0 as missing. footprints must be a non-empty PostgreSQL array.

Table 3 — Field-level coverage cards

Each card titleOne normalized `scity` bucket found in Unidata.
Row count lineHow many Unidata rows belong to that bucket.
Attribute rowsCompleteness inside <strong>that bucket only</strong>—percent of rows with usable values.
Hazard flagsShare of rows where liquefaction, landslide, and Alquist fault columns are all non-null.
Footprints non-emptyShare where the footprint geometry array has at least one entry.

Table 4 — Top gaps (missing baseline)

scityBuckets with the largest counts of unmatched baseline residential parcels.
MissingHow many baseline residential rows still lack a Unidata partner.
Coverage %Matched ÷ baseline residential rows for that bucket—low values highlight remediation priorities.

Table 5 — Weakest fields

PurposePrioritize engineering + data vendor follow-up.
ColumnsSame meaning as Table 2 but sorted so the lowest completeness fields appear first.
